title: Ananda's grief
hook: Ananda's verses after the passing: the friend is gone, all directions are dark (Theragatha, Ananda)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sariputta waited for his time as a worker waits for wages. Your line was as a servant waits for wages. Did you wait for something without checking on it? Today, the one left behind to do the waiting. Day eight hundred five.

Ananda was the Buddha's attendant. Tradition says he walked beside the teacher for years, looked after his needs, and remembered what he taught. We've been hearing calm voices in the brothers' book, men who have put the burden down. Ananda's verses hold a moment when the ground goes out from under him. A friend is gone. The teacher is gone. And all the directions go dark. Today we sit with that moment, and with what he found to hold on to.
screen: `THE BUDDHA'S ATTENDANT.` → `THE GROUND GOES OUT.` → `WHAT HE HELD ON TO.`

segments.voice: First, the line. All the directions are dark, he says. The teachings aren't clear to me. The good friend has gone, and everything seems dark. Second, whose death. The verses speak of a friend gone and of a teacher passed away. Tradition links these lines to the death of Sariputta, whose calm we heard yesterday, and to the passing of the Buddha. In one sutta, when word of Sariputta's death reaches Ananda, he tells the Buddha that his body feels unsteady, the directions aren't clear to him, and the teachings won't come to mind. Third, what's surprising. This sits in a book of freed men. And here is a long-time follower, saying grief has knocked the teaching right out of his head. The collection keeps his words as they are. Fourth, what he does with it. In the same verses, Ananda says that for one whose friend has gone and whose teacher has passed, there's no friend like mindfulness of the body. When the people are gone, what's left to hold is this breath, this body, here. And in the sutta, the Buddha answers him with what he had always taught: everything dear and pleasing will change and be parted from us. How could it be otherwise? He doesn't scold the grief. He reminds Ananda where to stand inside it. Grief, in these verses, isn't kept out of the practice. It's where the practice goes next.
screen: `ALL THE DIRECTIONS ARE DARK.` · `A FRIEND GONE, A TEACHER GONE.` · `THE BOOK KEEPS HIS WORDS.` · `NO FRIEND LIKE THE BODY'S MINDFULNESS.` · then, large: `ALL DIRECTIONS DARK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember a friend who's gone. Gone might mean died, or moved away, or simply drifted. Let one face come. Notice where you feel it: the chest, the throat, behind the eyes. Don't push it off, and don't dig for more. Then, like Ananda, rest some of your attention in the body itself: the weight in the chair, the breath going in and out. The friend in the mind, the breath in the body, both at once. If it gets too heavy, open your eyes and look around the room. The bell holds the time.
Ananda's grief. The attendant's verses when friend and teacher had gone: all directions dark, and mindfulness of the body as the friend that stays. Today's word.

Your line: all directions dark. Today, if someone near you is grieving, don't hurry them toward the light; just stay close. And look back at this week's lines: the rains came, once despised, the moon from the cloud, when will it be, these hills delight me, as a servant waits for wages, and now all directions dark. Day eight hundred five.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often turn to Ananda's grief, and the Buddha's reply about the parting from all that is dear, when they speak with people who are mourning, and some point to his verse on mindfulness of the body as a friend that stays.

myth: the Theragatha leaves out the elders' grief
Ananda's verses keep it: all the directions are dark, the teachings aren't clear.
Ananda says there's no friend like mindfulness of the body
for one whose friend and teacher are gone, he says, that is the friend that's left.
in the sutta, the Buddha scolds Ananda for grieving
he reminds him that everything dear will change and be parted from us.

fork.setup: you're Ananda. word comes that Sariputta has died, and everything goes dark. what do you do?
options: say nothing. a monk shouldn't grieve.
go to the Buddha and tell him how it is.
fork.reveal: in the sutta he tells the Buddha his body feels unsteady and the directions aren't clear to him. the Buddha answers with the teaching on parting from all that is dear.

original.note: Pali: disa, a direction. Ananda says all the directions are dark to him.

trapdoor: what you thought: a saint who was never shaken.
what it means: Ananda, when friend and teacher are gone, says all directions are dark, and turns to mindfulness of the body.
what a scholar hears: tradition links the verses to Sariputta's death and the Buddha's passing; in a sutta, Ananda tells the Buddha the directions aren't clear to him.

notes: Thag 17.3 (vv. 1018–1050 as remembered), around v. 1034–1035: 'all the directions are dark, the teachings are not clear to me; the good friend has gone...'; 'for one whose friend has gone, whose teacher has passed, there is no friend like mindfulness of the body'. Confirm wording and numbering.
Linking the verses to Sariputta's death and the Buddha's passing is attributed to tradition (commentary). Confirm.

SN 47.13: Ananda's body feels 'drugged'/unsteady, directions unclear, teachings not coming to mind; the Buddha's reply on separation from all that is dear. Confirm the paraphrase and that 'he doesn't scold' is a fair reading.
'Tradition says he walked beside the teacher for years' carries no number; confirm.
Week end (days 799–805): the carry looks back at the week's lines from the index.
Original: दिसा (disa); confirm Devanagari and stress.
Editor: 'the brothers' book is full of calm voices' softened to 'we've been hearing calm voices', so no sweeping claim about the whole collection.
Auditor (fresh review): howItsDone's unsourced 'mindfulness of the body is a common practice in grief' replaced with a softer claim tied to the verse.
